title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM (declared: gpt-5-mini) on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used a shared initial candidate (both conditions reuse the same generation) and allowed at most one automated repair call per failed candidate. Execution used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implementing binary full_intent_constraint_validation. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.996667), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered target effect (0.10, ≈80% power) was unattainable because the shared initial generator produced a near‑ceiling baseline and the guarded repair stage engaged exactly once. We (a) explain how these arithmetic and execution facts produce the null confirmatory outcome, (b) state which preregistered secondary analyses were not executed and why, (c) provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for future confirmatory tests, and (d) publish the authoritative artifacts for deterministic reproduction (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to assist and automate network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior empirical reports show LLMs can synthesize plausible configuration fragments but often produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors. Architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic verification and targeted automated repair—generate–validate–repair (GVR)—are widely advocated to reduce misconfiguration risk. However, the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that (1) couple explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics suitable for confirmatory inference, and (2) use sealed preregistration to avoid post‑hoc design changes. We implemented a preregistered study (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) that produces a deterministic synthetic task bank, a snapshot validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0), and a paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass generator using a shared‑initial generation design. The final, preregistered research question was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does a GVR pipeline increase per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent comprehensive surveys and reviews document growing interest in LLMs for network management and highlight core challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, and the need for verification—that bear on operational deployment [https://openalex.org/W4406137434; https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical studies demonstrate that out‑of‑the‑box LLMs can generate router configurations but frequently require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193; 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Prototype GVR and tool‑assisted prompting approaches can improve final correctness in focused settings [https://openalex.org/W4404652946], but published demonstrations are dataset‑specific and limited in scale. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts further motivate guarded architectures and deterministic validators for operational NetOps workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600; https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our contribution is a sealed, archived proof‑of‑concept benchmark plus a confirmatory paired run tying a deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under tightly specified retry and budget rules.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary hypothesis. We froze the experimental design before execution (preregistration id ac-2026-003-prereg-v1; preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration specified task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness handling, the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and a conservative repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate). Task bank. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, a required_sequence, and a difficulty label; device counts range 3–50 and use abstracted multi‑vendor device models. Validator semantics. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = v5.0) enforces full_intent_constraint_validation as a stateless snapshot checker: parse candidate commands into canonical field operations, enforce required_sequence and workflow_policies (ordering, group/mutual‑exclusion constraints), preserve unspecified state when requested, compute implied final_state, and return a binary valid flag with diagnostic violations and a validator trace. Shared‑initial paired design and repair budget. For each task we produced a single shared initial candidate that served both as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline’s initial candidate. If validation failed the guarded pipeline could invoke up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This design isolates repair value by preventing the guarded condition from sampling independent alternative initial candidates. Model configuration and deterministic execution. The declared model was gpt-5-mini, executed through the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with provider = "openai_responses". The archived model configuration records requested_model = "gpt-5-mini", max_output_tokens = 2000, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, reasoning_effort = "minimal" (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Provider traces were archived to allow deterministic reproduction (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Preregistered analysis. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on the N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness treatments and sensitivity analyses were preregistered; the run completed with no missing or excluded pairs.
sections.results: Execution accounting and provider audit. The execution manifest records: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00; completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00; planned_episode_count = 600; completed_episode_count = 600; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); artifact_hash_count = 2108. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 301 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, confirming the guarded repair stage executed exactly once across N=300 tasks. Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. All summarized analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55). Discordant pair and repair trace location. The single repair provider trace is the unique entry in execution/raw_results.jsonl whose provider stage field equals "repair"; execution/raw_results.jsonl is the authoritative per‑call provider trace container (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Extracting that single record deterministically yields the repair provider trace object and the discordant pair_id recorded therein; auditors can locate the discordant pair by searching execution/raw_results.jsonl for the record with stage=="repair" and reading its pair_id field. (Provider_call_audit stage_counts and the execution manifest cross‑reference permit deterministic lookup; the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json provide the mapping between provider calls and pair indices.) Why the preregistered target effect was unattainable. The preregistered power calculation assumed a substantive baseline failure rate such that a 0.10 absolute paired improvement could be detected with N=300. Observed baseline ≈0.997 makes that target effect arithmetically impossible: with marginal totals fixed the absolute maximum paired gain is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed difference), so detection of a 0.10 gain cannot occur regardless of analysis. The exact McNemar test depends only on discordant pairs (n10 and n01); with n10=1 and n01=0 the two‑sided exact p returned by the preregistered executor is 1.0—this numeric p reflects paucity of discordance rather than analytical error. The paired bootstrap CI better summarizes practical uncertainty under near‑ceiling margins.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under the sealed design (shared initial generation, deterministic snapshot validator, repair budget ≤1), the guarded GVR pipeline produced only a marginal improvement because the shared initial generator already produced validator‑passing candidates for 299/300 tasks; the guarded repair stage engaged only once. This outcome quantifies a boundary condition: when baseline generator correctness is near ceiling and repair budgets are tightly constrained, localized automated repair provides negligible marginal benefit. It does not imply GVR pipelines are broadly unhelpful—rather, it shows the conditions under which their marginal value is small. Missing preregistered secondary analyses. The preregistration included secondary_estimands such as per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions. These secondary estimands were not meaningfully executed as formal inferential reports because the confirmatory run produced essentially no failures beyond a single discordant improvement (n10=1), leaving insufficient variance for informative effect‑size estimation or subgroup inference; accordingly the archived analysis contains no substantive secondary_results. This omission is disclosed here and recorded in the analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json). Artifact‑grounded recommendations. The archived bundle supports concrete modifications that would render repair efficacy measurable in future confirmatory runs: (A) increase baseline difficulty (harder tasks or adversarial seeds) to raise initial failure rates (the execution logs show 299/300 initial successes); (B) allow iterative repair budgets or multi‑step repair triggers so repairs can engage when needed; (C) permit multiple independent initial generations per task to evaluate selection/reranking strategies; (D) adopt stateful/emulation validators modeling ordered side effects and temporal constraints to expose runtime failure modes; (E) include explicit adversarial test cases to exercise prompt‑hardening defenses. Each recommendation maps to archived execution facts (provider call counts, per‑task difficulty labels, and validator traces). Threats to validity. Internal: the shared initial design controls generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baselines or selection strategies; repair engagement was minimal. Construct: the validator enforces snapshot intent constraints but omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and in‑flight temporal behavior. External: synthetic tasks (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor) and a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant outcomes (n10=1) prevents robust subgroup or failure‑mode inference. Reproducibility note. The authoritative reproduction artifacts are archived: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) contains the provider traces including the unique repair record; execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) records the declared model and invocation settings; the preregistration artifact (SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765) fixes the design. Auditors can deterministically extract the discordant pair_id by locating the single entry where stage=="repair" in execution/raw_results.jsonl and reading its pair_id and provider trace fields.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that a GVR pipeline would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10, ≈80% power) was not supported because the shared initial generator produced a near‑ceiling baseline and the guarded repair stage executed only once (provider stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). We archive the preregistration, execution manifest, raw provider traces, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can instantiate harder settings (increased task difficulty, iterative repairs, multi‑generation baselines, multi‑model comparisons) that will permit rigorous evaluation of when and how GVR pipelines deliver measurable operational benefit.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
